Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

In Texas, a TWIA windstorm policy requires flood insurance when any part of the property is in a V, VE or V1-V30 zone, NFIP cover is available for it, and the structure was built, altered, remodeled or enlarged after September 1, 2009.

13.1% of Montgomery County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 13.1% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 45.3% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Zone X19,24286.9%
Zone AE (high-risk)2,76912.5%
Other high-risk zones (A, VE)1230.6%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones10.0%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Flood map: FEMA's current flood map for unincorporated Montgomery County took effect August 18, 2014. FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Montgomery County has 47 map panels, the oldest in effect since August 18, 2014 and the newest since August 18, 2014. FEMA has revised that map by 49 Letters of Map Revision, 19 of them in effect since January 1, 2021. FEMA's map service lists 767 rulings for owners here who asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone (Letters of Map Amendment): 610 took the building or some or all of the lot out, 55 found it already outside the zone as mapped, 70 were denied, 32 other or mixed. FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one. These are rulings for owners who chose to apply, so they are not the odds for your home, and FEMA's map service gives no dates for them. They are counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here. FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

Flood insurance cost in Montgomery County, Texas

In Montgomery County, typically about $1,005 a year ($84 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $708 and $1,235. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $708 · Typical $1,005 · A quarter pay over $1,235 · A tenth pay $1,309 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 19,310 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay. Property that is not your primary residence, such as a second home, a rental you own or a non-residential building, pays a higher federal surcharge: $250 a year, against $25 for a primary home.

Source: floodsmart.gov, law.cornell.edu (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Exceptions to the thirty-day wait, what a policy won't pay (wind, outside belongings, living costs), FEMA aid vs insurance, appeals, the substantial-damage rebuilding rule and the rules at a closing: the NFIP rules in full, each with its official source.

Your state's insurance regulator: Texas Department of Insurance.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Montgomery County, Texas: what floods pay out

Floods in Montgomery County have led to 12,643 NFIP flood claims and $631.7 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2017, 2016 and 2019.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2017 ($248,238,864), 2016 ($91,196,333), 2019 ($89,853,595). Total paid $631,710,978. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: of the 5,677 claims here with a flood zone on the claim, losses 2016–2025, 55.0% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D), and they got 47.0% of the dollars paid on those claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 55.0% of the 12,282 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 12,282 policies reporting one)55.0%Texas: 35.8%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)89.1%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 10,717 claims paid with a damage figure)9.1%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 11, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $964 a year (Zone X) to $1,364 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone X$96417,222
Zone AE$1,3642,013
Zone A$1,20274

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

35.3% of single-family primary-home policies in Montgomery County have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $791, full-risk $811 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$791
  • Median full-risk premium$811
  • Pay below full-risk35.3% of 19,310Texas: 42.3%

Yearly cap: Except for the Emergency Program discount, statutory discounts gradually phase out through an annual increase cap discount at each renewal date until the policy reaches its full-risk premium. By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year; the rate for some property, including homes that are not a primary residence and business property, rises 25% a year until that group's average rate reaches the level the law sets (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)). FloodSmart puts the limit at 18 to 25% a year for most policyholders. It usually does not apply to new policies, raising your coverage or lowering your deductible can go past it, and fees and surcharges are added on top.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Inland: FEMA models roughly $94.4 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 55% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 11, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $134.6 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,260 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 11, 2026.
